@danmosemsft How should I treat for instance the strange documentation of X509CertificateCollection.Remove and X509Certificate2Collection.Remove?
Documentation for the first one throws ArgumentException if not found, so that one is easy, just throw, but the one for 2, says throws ArgumentNullException in the case of null input, but does not throw ArgumentException if not found.

And another issue, is that neither CollectionBase or IList says anything about throwing ArgumentNullException if the input argument is null and currently CollectionBase does throw in that case. Should I fix that as well?

so @eiriktsarpalis and @danmosemsft, what's next then?
Seems like there is a lot of potential update of documentation or pushing this through and see what comes out on the other end? Just look at my question about the certificate collections, two remove methods and two different sets of exceptions thrown.

> so @eiriktsarpalis and @danmosemsft, what's next then?

As noted in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/46166#discussion_r551474042, there are too many `CollectionBase` subclasses that depend on the current `IList.Remove` behaviour (which is typically accessed via its [protected `List` property](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/e49c9eb329743e93106296a723bfc362d4e2610f/src/libraries/System.Collections.NonGeneric/src/System/Collections/CollectionBase.cs#L38-L41), making it more commonly used than a typical explicit interface implementation like the one in #36926). It suggests to me that other codebases deriving from `CollectionBase` might follow the same pattern, so we risk breaking their code with this change.

I would therefore recommend we not make this change, since the benefits (fixing an interface inconsistency in a non-generic collection) don't seem to outweigh the risks. @danmosemsft thoughts?

I agree with @eiriktsarpalis.  This is largely impacting legacy types that we have for compatibility, e.g. non-generic collections, CodeDom, etc., and has been around for almost two decades.  It's also different from #36926 IMO: beyond that being a generic collection and this being a non-generic collection, `ReadOnlyDictionary<>` generally isn't used as a base type that others inherit behavior from, whereas `CollectionBase` is.
I can close this pr then, and update the documentation for the collections I found with wrong info instead then ;)

issue_context.title: CollectionBase implements IList.Remove to throw, contrary to docs
comments: I couldn't figure out the best area label to add to this issue. If you have write-permissions please help me learn by adding exactly one [area label](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/area-owners.md).

Tagging subscribers to this area: @eiriktsarpalis
Notify danmosemsft if you want to be subscribed.
I feel that we should probably just update the docs to reflect the current behaviour. Changing the behaviour could break users.
Changing interface implementations to match the contract now has precedent with #36926. We should consider doing the same thing here /cc @stephentoub

As illustrated in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/46166#issuecomment-754168515 many classes inheriting from `CollectionBase` depend on the current throwing behaviour. So in the interest of maintaining compatibility, we will preserve the current behaviour even though it is inconsistent with `IList` specification.

review_comments:
I'm seeing a few issues with this PR:

* The change explicitly throws an exception when the value has not been found, however #39703 proposes that no exception should be thrown at all.
* More importantly, the proposal concerns the explicit interface implementation `IList.Remove(object)` found in the [`CollectionBase` class](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/144cac3d0ce162444452a5dcc837b904fe149ef4/src/libraries/System.Collections.NonGeneric/src/System/Collections/CollectionBase.cs#L170). This is an unrelated public method defined by a subclass of CollectionBase.

The CodeTypeReferenceCollection remove method documentation says it is supposed to throw on not found, and the existing code was relaying on the "bug" in collectionbase that was throwing when it wasn't supposed to. The build pipeline/tests was failing after my first fix since it was expecting this exception

This comment will be the same for all my changes to random collection in this pr. I have went over all failing tests and fixes either the test not to expect a throw or fixed the implementation if the documentation said it is supposed to throw on not found

Oh I see, thanks for the clarification. I had not realized that the protected `List` property was returning the collection instance itself. The prevalence of this pattern (and accompanying failing tests) suggests to me that the throwing behaviour CollectionBase is part of the informal spec, and changing it might break other users too.
